'''Jessamine Sophia Whitney''' (1880 – March 11, 1941) was an American statistician and public health professional, who worked at the [[American Lung Association|National Tuberculosis Association]] for 22 years. 
 
== Early life and education ==
Whitney was born in [[Norwich, New York]], in 1880, the daughter of Dr. W. W. Whitney. She attended [[Binghamton High School|Binghamton Central High School]] in the class of 1897, and [[State University of New York at Oneonta|Oneonta Normal School]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33500259/jessamine_s_whitney_1936/|title=Miss Jessamine Whitney Breaks Her Arm in Fall|date=January 27, 1936|work=Press and Sun-Bulletin|access-date=July 3, 2019|page=3|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She studied mathematics and economics and earned a bachelor's degree in 1905 from [[Cornell University]], with further studies in [[actuarial science]] at [[New York University]].<ref name=":0">[https://www.atsjournals.org/doi/abs/10.1164/art.1941.43.6.849?journalCode=art "Obituary: Jessamine S. Whitney, 1880–1941"] ''American Review of Tuberculosis'', 43(6), pp. 849–850</ref> She was active in the New York College Women's Suffrage Association,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://newspaperarchive.com/science-clipping-feb-15-1914-1248123/|title=They Call her a Woman with a Mission; Her Life has been Replete with Missions|last=Craig|first=Britt|date=February 15, 1914|work=Atlanta Constitution|access-date=July 3, 2019|page=29|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> and served as president of the New York and Washington chapters of the Cornell Women's Club.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://cdsun.library.cornell.edu/?a=d&d=CDS19410318.2.27&|title=Miss J. S. Whitney '05 Dies Recently in N. Y.|date=March 18, 1941|work=Cornell Daily Sun|access-date=July 3, 2019}}</ref>

== Career ==
Whitney taught English in Puerto Rico as a young woman; during that time, in 1904, she was described as "the first woman to drive an automobile in Porto Rico": "she very quickly mastered it, finally taking complete charge and guiding the vehicle the greater part of the distance" from [[Ponce, Puerto Rico|Ponce]] to [[San Juan, Puerto Rico|San Juan]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Morgan|first=Angela|date=April 1904|title=Automobiling for Women|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XXVUAAAAYAAJ&q=Jessamine%20Whitney&pg=PA537|journal=The World To-day|volume=6|pages=537}}</ref> She returned to Puerto Rico in 1931 for the National Tuberculosis Association.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Aided Porto Rico's Health|date=April 7, 1931|work=The New York Times|page=6|id={{ProQuest|<!--ProQuest data goes here--> }}}}</ref>
[[File:JessamineSWhitneyMotorAge.jpg|alt=An automobile with four passengers in 1904, including a woman in a long white dress in front.|thumb|Jessamine S. Whitney in an automobile in Puerto Rico, from a 1904 publication.]]
Whitney worked at the [[United States Census Bureau]] in 1909, compiling tables of data on infant mortality, and for the [[Bureau of Labor Statistics|United States Bureau of Labor Statistics]], studying child labor in cotton mills; she was also a statistician at the [[United States Shipping Board]].<ref name=":0" /> In 1913 and 1914, she made a survey of conditions for [[tuberculosis]] in Georgia, under the auspices of the Raoul Foundation.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33502459/jessamine_whitney_1941/|title=Jessamine Whitney, Health Expert, Dies|date=March 13, 1941|work=The Atlanta Constitution|access-date=July 3, 2019|page=15|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>
[[File:JessamineSWhitney1914.jpg|alt=A man and a woman standing on a baseball diamond. The man is wearing a player's uniform; the woman is wearing a loose, tailored suit and an umpire's mask, and holds a bat.|thumb|Jessamine S. Whitney as an umpire in a 1914 charity baseball game (the player in the foreground is Pat Witherbee).]]
Whitney began working at the National Tuberculosis Association in 1918, as "research secretary", a title eventually changed to "chief statistician".<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1941/03/12/archives/jessamine-whitney-statistician-since-1918-for-the-national.html|title=Jessamine Whitney; Statistician Since 1918 for the National Association Dies|date=1941-03-12|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-07-03|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4Y2oDQAAQBAJ&q=Jessamine%20Whitney&pg=PT94|title=Death 101: A Workbook for Educating and Healing, 2nd edition|last=Straub|first=Sandra Helene|date=2016-12-05|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781351844598|pages=62–65|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/womenscientistsi0000ross|url-access=registration|quote=Jessamine Whitney.|title=Women Scientists in America: Struggles and Strategies to 1940|last=Rossiter|first=Margaret W.|date=1982|publisher=JHU Press|isbn=9780801825095|pages=[https://archive.org/details/womenscientistsi0000ross/page/379 379]|language=en}}</ref> She wrote pamphlets and articles for the Association, including "The Costs of Tuberculosis" (1921, with [[Louis Israel Dublin]]),<ref>Dublin, Louis I., and Jessamine S. Whitney (April 1921). [https://books.google.com/books?id=tfhFAQAAMAAJ&dq=Jessamine+Whitney&pg=PA178 "The Costs of Tuberculosis"] ''American Review of Tuberculosis'' 5:178–184.</ref> "The Rural Health Demonstration" (1924),<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Whitney|first=Jessamine S.|date=1924-09-06|title=The Rural Health Demonstration|url=https://www.milbank.org/quarterly/articles/the-rural-health-demonstration-4/|journal=The Milbank Quarterly|language=en-US|volume=2|issue=3|pages=20–22}}</ref> "Facts and Figures about Tuberculosis" (1931),<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Whitney|first=Jessamine|date=June 1931|title=Facts and Figures about Tuberculosis|journal=American Journal of Nursing|language=en-US|volume=31|issue=6|pages=784|issn=0002-936X|doi=10.1097/00000446-193106000-00066|hdl=2027/umn.31951000089196d|hdl-access=free}}</ref> "Official Report of Childhood Type of Tuberculosis" (1934),<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Whitney|first=Jessamine S.|date=1934-08-01|title=Official Reporting of Childhood Type of Tuberculosis|journal=American Journal of Public Health and the Nation's Health|volume=24|issue=8|pages=850–852|doi=10.2105/AJPH.24.8.850|pmid=18014033|pmc=1558828|issn=0002-9572}}</ref> "Tuberculosis among Nurses" (1935),<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Whitney|first=Jessamine S.|date=1935|title=Tuberculosis among Nurses: A Summary of the Literature|journal=The American Journal of Nursing|volume=35|issue=4|pages=367–375|doi=10.2307/3411551|issn=0002-936X|jstor=3411551}}</ref> and "The Need for Statistics on Rehabilitation" (1937). She worked with Alba M. Edwards of the Bureau of the Census on occupational health research, and standardizing occupational categories for mortality studies.<ref name=":2" /> She documented "tuberculosis migration," showing how Easterners with tuberculosis moving to the American Southwest for the supposed health benefits of a drier climate was creating a strain on resources in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Colorado, and California.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=LphJAQAAMAAJ&dq=Jessamine+Whitney&pg=PA423 "Home Cure versus 'Change of Climate'"] ''The American Journal of Public Health'' (May 1922): 423–424.</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33502618/jessamine_s_whitney_1922/|title=State Climate is Favorable|date=March 23, 1922|work=Alma Record|access-date=July 3, 2019|page=5|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33502690/jessamine_s_whitney_1929/|title=Great Burden of White Plague Told as Statistician Declares 10,000 Wanderers are Victims|date=July 2, 1929|work=The San Bernardino County Sun|access-date=July 3, 2019|page=3|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

In 1929 and 1938, Whitney represented the United States at the meeting of the International Conference on the Classification of Causes of Death; she was the only woman delegate from any country to attend in 1929,<ref name=":0" /> and one of only three women delegates at the 1938 meeting.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news|title=Miss Whitney, Pioneer in Field, Sees Romance in Dry Statistics|date=April 9, 1939|work=The New York Times|page=D5|id={{ProQuest|<!--ProQuest data goes here--> }}}}</ref> In 1935 she was described as the "ranking woman vital statistician of this country, and probably of the world."<ref name=":4">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33499886/jessamine_s_whitney_1935/|title=Statistician Figures Ways to Curb Tuberculosis|last=McBride|first=Mary Margaret|date=August 9, 1935|work=The Sheboygan Press|access-date=July 3, 2019|page=6|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

== Baseball ==
Whitney was a self-described baseball fan from childhood.<ref name=":4" /> She compiled statistics on players and teams, and predicted winners based on her own calculations.<ref name=":3" /> In 1914, she was recruited to be an umpire at a charity baseball game at the [[National Conference of Charities and Correction]] meeting in Memphis.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=July 18, 1914|title=The Lady Umpire of Charity Baseball|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QigrAAAAYAAJ&q=Jessamine&pg=PA422|journal=The Survey|volume=32|pages=422}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Whitney died after suffering a heart attack at her desk in 1941, aged 61 years, in New York.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33502803/jessamine_s_whitney_1941/|title=Top Statistics Expert Dead|date=March 12, 1941|work=Press and Sun-Bulletin|access-date=July 3, 2019|page=13|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> Her gravesite was at Vestal Cemetery in [[Endicott, New York]].<ref name=":1" />
